positive: Many commenters are excited and eager to pre-order as soon as it opens, with some planning to order right at launch and others struggling to wait.
Several say they want it despite not needing it, and cost doesn't seem to put them off.
Buyers mention specific choices, mostly the white finish with large storage and unlocked, and some are drawn by its feel and video-viewing use.
Many commenters say they are excited for release and plan to preorder or buy early, with some saying they're ready to pay right away.
Commenters like the design and the large pocketable screen, and several say a foldable from Apple is what they've wanted for a long time.
Some accept missing features or a weaker camera, while a few suggest later generations will be better but still plan to buy this one.
negative: Many commenters say the price is far too high, joking that buying the phone would cost them their savings or even a kidney.
Several would rather wait for a later version or see how durable the foldable screen proves, doubting a first-generation Apple model will be right.
Some mock the name and feature branding as odd or overhyped, and criticise Apple fans who buy it despite expressing indifference to its features.

positive: Most commenters say they still plan to buy, brushing off warnings against it and comparisons with Android rivals.
Drawbacks such as Touch ID and no telephoto lens are acknowledged, but several say they don't mind and prefer the interface.
The high price is the main concern raised, though some say interest-free financing or free coverage through retailers makes it manageable.
negative: Price is the dominant complaint: commenters see the phone as far too expensive, especially higher storage tiers once tax is included, and some urge a boycott.
Several argue the extras are pointless or wasteful, such as built-in magnetic charging that a case would cover, or gimmicky features.
Some see it as a copy of other foldables and say Android phones are better for cameras, so they would not buy it.

positive: Several commenters defend the high price, saying a foldable that works as two devices in one, with strong software, is worth paying more for.
Many say they care little about camera quality and would pay for the design, larger screen, multitasking and document or video use instead.
Some admit they can't afford it or aren't sure a foldable suits them, yet they are impressed by the fold animations and software.
negative: Many commenters say a price around two thousand for a phone is unreasonable, especially given current economic conditions and the cost of higher-storage versions.
Several feel the value is poor: modest storage on the base model, few cameras, and compromises such as limited dust and water protection.
Some worry about long-term durability and costly repairs from the fold, plus the need for a bulky case, making the investment feel risky.

positive: Many commenters on older phones, such as the 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16 Pro models, plan to upgrade to the Duo and say it feels like a worthwhile jump.
Several say they rarely use pro-level cameras and would rather have a bigger, more versatile screen. Some hope it will replace carrying a tablet or laptop.
Some see the Pro line as stale or less appealing, and expect the Duo to feel fresh. A few will keep a Pro for photos alongside it.
negative: Many commenters say the Duo's price is too high, especially given its camera and feature compromises, and they prefer the cheaper Pro Max.
Camera downgrades versus the 18 Pro line (fewer lenses, weaker telephoto and main sensor) are a frequent dealbreaker, particularly for people who prioritise photo and video.
Missing Face ID, uncertainty about a first-generation foldable, and little need for the inner screen lead many to wait for a later Duo or keep their current phone.

positive: Many commenters are current Samsung Fold owners who say they are happy with their device and plan to keep it.
Several longtime Samsung users admit they are surprised and impressed by what Apple achieved with its first foldable.
Some point out that Samsung's customisation and innovation remain strong, hoping Apple's entry pushes Samsung to bring back features like stylus support and water resistance.
negative: Many commenters say Apple is late and copying a foldable concept Samsung and others have sold for years, and that its launch presentation oversells the novelty.
Several complain the iPhone Duo is expensive, even costing more than Samsung's current Fold models in some places, so they expect top cameras and features.
Some compare specs: the Duo is seen as heavier and thicker than the Fold, and lacks a published fold durability rating. Others criticise Samsung's software and design.

positive: Many commenters praise Apple's software polish, especially the fold and unfold transition and animations, calling it a signature touch that sets the phone apart.
Several people say they were not interested in foldables until Apple made one, and are impressed or planning to pre-order, partly because of iOS simplicity and ecosystem loyalty.
Some see Apple as a late arrival that still executes well. Others note Android has offered similar features longer, and that rivals borrowing ideas benefits consumers.
negative: Many commenters say Apple lacks fresh ideas and copies features Android makers, especially Samsung, introduced years earlier, arriving late to foldables.
Commenters point out that Apple fans once dismissed foldables as gimmicks but now praise them once Apple makes one.
Others complain about high prices and the risk of buying a first-generation Apple product, expecting flaws and a quick successor.

positive: Many commenters praise the matte inner screen, saying it looks attractive, helps hide the crease, and suits long reading sessions.
The transition between the outer and inner screens when folding or unfolding is described as smooth, clean and impressive.
A larger screen in a pocket appeals to people, including for multitasking and bigger text, and some prefer a clean display without a camera cutout.
negative: Many doubt the inner display's quality: it looks less sharp than the front, and the matte anti-reflective finish and curved edges are disliked.
Commenters see the crease as downplayed, with the matte coating seen as a way to hide it. They also note that Apple relies on Samsung for the panel and that this adds to the price.
Concerns about durability and cost: foldable screens reportedly failing after about a year, expensive repairs or AppleCare charges, and a high price for only a slightly bigger screen.

positive: Commenters prefer a hidden under-display camera over a hole punch or notch, saying an uninterrupted full screen looks cleaner and matters more than critics suggest.
Many note that selfies would mostly be taken with the outer display camera, so the inner camera's lower quality matters little.
The matte inner display is praised as a smart way to hide the crease and give a smooth, premium look.
negative: Many commenters say under-display cameras give poor image quality, and some think the technology has been dropped for good reason.
The inner display draws complaints for looking grainy, having inaccurate colours, and having a matte finish instead of a glossy OLED look.
Some commenters would rather have different hardware, such as a third rear lens or stylus support, and dislike camera bumps that stop the phone lying flat.

positive: Commenters widely praise the opening and closing animation as smooth, clean and seamless, with many calling it clever or a standout feature.
Several credit the design team for the transition, especially the blur and see-through glass effect that makes the front panel appear transparent.
Some say the animation could drive sales and reflects Apple's polish, with even Samsung fans admitting it is impressive.
negative: Commenters mock the fold animation being treated as a headline feature, saying it reflects poorly on the phone's overall strengths.
Many call the animation a simple, gimmicky effect that loses appeal quickly and has little practical value.
Some note a visual glitch when closing, and say real differences like weight, thickness and pocketability matter more.

positive: Several people, including right-handed ones who use their left hand, say the concern is overblown and would barely affect daily use.
Some expect a software setting to mirror or rotate the layout for left-handed users, and a few are keen to buy the phone.
negative: Left-handed users feel the foldable's design favors right-handed use, with some saying they would find it awkward or frustrating.
Face ID placement and unlocking are a specific worry for left-handers, and one says they will wait for a later generation.
Several comments mock the 'holding it wrong' idea, suggesting left-handers are expected to adapt rather than the design adapting.

positive: Pencil support is a major selling point for several commenters, who see it as a deciding reason to buy the foldable.
Some want to sketch and paint on the phone, and hope apps like Procreate add support for it.
People coming from rival foldables say the lack of pen support there is a drawback, making Apple's version more appealing.
Reading, media, navigation, medical work and retro-style gaming are named as good uses for the unfolded size and flexible orientations.
Several viewers praise the software, side toolbar and button placement, and say the weaker cameras don't matter since they rarely use a phone for photos.
negative: Many see the foldable as essentially a small iPad in phone form, so they question the point when a regular iPad costs less.
The high price is a major objection: commenters call it poor value, a gimmick, or a niche device, and some suggest waiting for later generations.
Others doubt the design and practicality: the folded shape seems awkward, the crease may show over time, and the big screen may rarely get used.

positive: Many commenters are excited about the foldable design, calling it a refreshing, distinctive iPhone and the most interesting release in nearly a decade.
Commenters value the larger folding screen for multitasking, and some expect a titanium build to be durable and comfortable to hold.
Some want tougher glass protection and slimmer bezels, while a few are holding off, comparing it with rivals or waiting for next year's model.
negative: Many commenters say the foldable is very heavy, and that a case would make one-handed use awkward.
Several joke that Apple will pitch later models as thinner, lighter or with less visible crease, implying this first version is flawed.
Some dislike the name and the overall design, calling it a copy of rivals' foldables or saying a flip style would suit better.

positive: Many commenters are very excited and plan to buy or preorder the Duo, often as an emotional want rather than a practical need.
Viewers like the book-like opening, the hardware and software integration, and the nano texture that hides the fold crease.
negative: Price is a major objection: the Duo is seen as very expensive, especially for base storage and in some regions, with doubts about real demand.
Hardware is criticized as heavy, thick and compromised on cameras and durability, with worries about cases, an unbalanced camera bump and unknown reliability.
Rival foldables are viewed as better value or more capable, with disputes over chip claims, missing features, unclear specs and carrier lock-in terms.

positive: Commenters like the software and transitions, and think the unfolded layout suits reading and apps that are well designed for it.
Developer support is seen as a strength, with third-party apps such as Netflix adapting. Some expect better iPad apps as a side effect.
Several comments say the hype has made foldables more appealing, and that the software and app ecosystem will be the main draw.
negative: Commenters doubt the multitasking features are useful, saying the foldable is mostly hype and marketing for an exclusive, expensive device few people need.
Some say the app-dragging and window-arranging features resemble existing iPad software, and that portrait multitasking looks limited to pop-up video.
Others criticise hardware control choices, such as the programmable action button replacing the mute switch and the odd placement of the volume buttons.

positive: Some commenters prefer a fingerprint sensor, saying it unlocks faster and more reliably than face scanning, which they call a gimmick.
Privacy is a concern for some: they feel more at ease when the phone isn't constantly scanning their face.
Others praise the design as polished and say it makes them more interested in buying, though many comments drift to other topics like copying and cameras.
negative: Several commenters are disappointed the device reportedly lacks Face ID, with one saying it is why they would wait for later models.
Some feel the missing Face ID and other hardware cuts make the product seem incomplete or like a step back.
Other complaints concern wasted screen space and high pricing, which only loosely relate to biometric unlock.
